chunks: A number of our companions, from Ahmad ibn Abi Abdullah, who said:

Ibn Umm Maktum sought permission to enter upon the Prophet (peace be upon him and his family), and with him were Ayesha and Hafsa, so he said to them both, 'Arise and enter the room.' So they both said, 'He is blind.' So he said, 'If he does not see you, then you see him.'

key_terms.ابْنُ أُمِّ مَكْتُومٍ: Ibn Umm Maktum, a companion known for his blindness

ai.seo_question: What is the significance of Ibn Umm Maktum's visit to the Prophet regarding blindness and social equality?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi illustrates the Prophet’s (saww) practical application of social equity, where he rebukes Ayesha and Hafsa for their subtle bias against the blind companion, Ibn Umm Maktum. The Prophet’s response, 'If he does not see you, you see him,' underscores that physical disability does not diminish one's right to access or dignity, a principle deeply valued in Shia jurisprudence for inclusive community leadership. It serves as a foundational text for the permissibility and encouragement of blind individuals holding positions of authority and public engagement.

en.hubeali: A number of our companions, from Ahmad Bin Abu Abdullah who said,

‘Ibn Umm Maktoum sought permission to visit the Prophet<sup>as</sup>, and in his<sup>saww</sup> presence were Ayesha and Hafsa, so he<sup>saww</sup> said to them both, ‘Arise and enter the (other) room’. So they both said, ‘He is blind!’ So he<sup>saww</sup> said: ‘He cannot see the two of you, but you two can see him’.
en.sarwar: 2. A number of our people have narrated from Ahmad ibn abu ‘Abd Allah who has said the following:

“Once ibn ‘Umm Maktum asked permission from the Holy Prophet, O Allah, grant compensation to Muhammad and his family worthy of their services to Your cause, when ‘Ai’shah and Hafsah were with him. He (the Messenger of Allah) asked them to go to the room and they said, ‘He is blind.’ He (the Messenger of Allah) said, ‘If he cannot see you, you two can see him.’”
